records.table: Laird's Straight Apple Brandy Bottled in Bond is all apple, distilled in Virginia for the New Jersey house of Laird & Company and kept four years or more in charred oak before bottling at 100 proof. It is the apple brandy for a Jack Rose; neat, it pours baked apple.
records.story: The Laird family traces its line in Monmouth County, New Jersey, to a Scot from Fife who settled there in 1698, and by the house's account the family was making cider spirits, the old name for apple brandy, in colonial days. The story goes that George Washington (1732 to 1799) asked the family for its recipe, and a Laird served under him in the Continental Army. The firm dates itself to 1780, the year of the first commercial sale in its records. In 1849 fire destroyed the distillery at the Colts Neck Inn, and the fifth generation rebuilt it nearby at Scobeyville. Prohibition shut it; in 1933, as the house tells it, two brothers of the family reopened it under a permit to distil apple brandy for medicine. Applejack and apple brandy were long one spirit, until the family petitioned for a federal class of blended applejack, apple brandy cut with neutral grain spirit. From 1976 all distilling took place at North Garden, Virginia. The bonded bottling is the apple side of that history, and the bottle to reach for when an old recipe asks for applejack.

records.table: E&J VSOP Grand Blue is the California brandy of E. & J. Gallo, grape spirit aged at least two years in oak and bottled at 80 proof. It pours vanilla, maple and brown spice, a soft brandy for a Sidecar or a Brandy Alexander.
records.story: Ernest Gallo (1909 to 2007) and his younger brother Julio Gallo (1910 to 1993) founded their winery in Modesto, in the Central Valley of California, in 1933, the year Prohibition ended. Over the next four decades it grew into one of the large wine companies of the United States, and the brothers turned to brandy. As the company tells it, they spent five years testing and tasting at their Fresno distillery before they settled on a process, and the first E&J Brandy was bottled in March 1975, aged two years in oak. The initials are the brothers' own. The range came to hold a VS, a VSOP and an XO, with flavoured brandies such as vanilla beside them. The VSOP borrows its letters from Cognac, where they promise that no eau-de-vie in the blend is younger than four years; E&J gives its own figure of at least two. That is the lesson of the bottle for a bartender: on an American brandy the grade is the house's word, while the class and the strength are the law's.

records.table: The Christian Brothers VS is a grape brandy with a California past, made by Heaven Hill and rested at least two years in former bourbon barrels. It pours vanilla, maple and dried fruit, a brandy for the highball and the Brandy Old Fashioned.
records.story: The Christian Brothers are the De La Salle Brothers, a Catholic order of teachers, and the brand dates itself to 1882, when the order was making wine in California at Martinez, east of San Francisco Bay. In 1930 the brothers bought the Mont La Salle property in the hills above Napa and moved their winery there. Their brandy came later than the brand's date suggests: a historical marker at Mont La Salle dates the first Christian Brothers Brandy to 1940. Wine and brandy carried the order's name for half a century, until in 1989 the brothers sold the business to Heublein. In 1999 Heaven Hill bought the brandy together with the Bernheim Distillery in Louisville, after the fire of 1996 at its Bardstown distillery, and from then on the brandy rested in former bourbon barrels and was bottled in Bardstown. That makes the VS a plain lesson behind the bar: much American brandy is grape spirit from the West, rested in bourbon wood in bourbon country.

records.table: Korbel California Brandy comes from the Russian River sparkling wine house at Guerneville, column distilled from Colombard and Chenin Blanc and aged in charred American oak. Wisconsin has long built its Brandy Old Fashioned on it, butterscotch and cinnamon in the glass.
records.story: Three Czech brothers of the Korbel family came to California from Bohemia and settled on the Russian River at Guerneville in Sonoma County, where the house dates its winery to 1882. In 1889, seven years after the first of its sparkling wines by the house's account, Korbel began shipping a California brandy. The story goes that the brothers poured their wine and brandy at the Chicago fair of 1893, and that visitors from Milwaukee, many of them from central Europe, took a liking to the brandy of their Bohemian neighbours and carried it home to Wisconsin, where it went into the Old Fashioned in place of whiskey. It is a legend, but Wisconsin has long been the brandy's stronghold. Prohibition halted the trade, and in 1954 the Korbel family sold the company to a family of winemakers, who built its sparkling wine into the name most guests know. Behind a bar the brandy is the reason a guest from Wisconsin orders a Brandy Old Fashioned sweet, and the bottle to reach for when one does.

records.story: Copper & Kings opened in 2014, founded by a couple who had built and sold drinks companies before and who chose Louisville over the West Coast for an American brandy house. They set up in Butchertown, the city's old quarter of butchers and stockyards, with copper pot stills and one aim: brandy distilled from American wine and rested in Kentucky bourbon barrels, in the heart of bourbon country. While their own spirit aged, early bottlings were blended with brandy from other producers, as the founders told reporters. The range grew with Butchertown Brandy, launched in 2015, and Floodwall, an apple brandy named for the city's floodwall, in 2016. In 2018 Constellation Brands bought a minority stake, and in 2020 it bought the rest of the company. In 2025 the Bourdon Spirits Company, a Louisville firm, bought Copper & Kings from Constellation, and distilling went on in Butchertown. For a bartender the house is the counterweight to the big California brands: pot still brandy, bourbon wood and Kentucky.
